title: Precorrections
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark's DistillED newsletter explains "precorrection" - a brief, positively framed reminder of expected behaviour delivered in the seconds before a moment a teacher already knows tends to go wrong. Drawing on Colvin, Sugai, and Patching's 1993 framework, the piece distinguishes precorrection (proactive, timed to a known pattern) from ordinary correction (reactive, delivered after the fact), and lays out a five-step sequence for building one: spot the pattern, name the expected behaviour, adjust the setup, rehearse and prompt, then reinforce and check. Clark cites school-wide research showing that precorrection paired with active supervision reduced problem behaviour at predictable transition points like building entry and the walk to the cafeteria, as well as classroom-level studies showing gains from brief verbal or visual reminders before class. The piece is explicit about what precorrection is not - a threat, a static rule on the wall, a one-off fix, or generic front-loading - and argues that as students become fluent the reminder itself should fade from a full sentence to a gesture to nothing at all.
points: Precorrection reframes classroom-management theory by treating misbehaviour the way teachers already treat academic errors: reteach the correct response before the next attempt rather than correcting only after the fact.

The five-step sequence (spot the pattern, name the expected behaviour, adjust the setup, rehearse and prompt, reinforce and check) turns a vague 'stay calm' instruction into an observable, fadeable routine.
School-wide trials pairing precorrection with active supervision showed measurable drops in problem behaviour at predictable transition points like building entry and the walk to the cafeteria.

The technique is explicitly not a warning, a wall poster, or front-loading — it targets one specific, previously observed pattern with positively framed language delivered seconds before the risk moment.
quotes: Precorrection is a quick, planned reminder of expected behaviour, delivered just before a moment you already know tends to go wrong. It is not a warning, or a rule on the wall, but a prompt timed to land right before the trouble spot.
When a student keeps making the same maths mistake, we don't just keep correcting it after the fact — we reteach the rule before they attempt the next problem.

Correction procedures are consequent manipulations designed to signal and stop inappropriate behavior after it occurs, while precorrection procedures are antecedent manipulations designed to prevent the occurrence of predictable inappropriate behavior.
A rehearsal can be as brief as asking a student to state what's expected, given in the minute before the target moment rather than earlier in the day.
The goal isn't a classroom full of reminders. It's a classroom where the moments that used to go wrong quietly stop needing them.

As the expected behaviour becomes the normal behaviour, the reminder should shrink — from a full sentence, to a gesture, to nothing at all. If you're still precorrecting the same moment six months from now, the pattern probably needs a different kind of attention.
Precorrection doesn't work in isolation. It sits in a healthy classroom culture made up of clear expectations, consistent routines, that are used deliberately.
